Kolam dates back to 500 BCE, mentioned in Sangam literature.
There are three main types of Kolam categories named Sikku Kolam, Pulli Kolam and Rangoli.
Where they originated: Tamil Nadu (South India).
The Origin Story: These practices originated in prehistoric tribal and early agricultural communities in ancient Tamilakam. They began as an ecological and mathematical necessity.
Ancient Tamils drew grids of dots (Pulli) using edible rice flour to feed ants and birds.
They connected or looped around the dots because they believed closed loops trapped evil spirits at the doorstep, preventing them from entering the house.
Sikku (or Kambi) Kolam: Place dots, but never let your lines touch them. Instead, one continuous line twists, turns, and loops around the dots without breaking.
Pulli Kolam: Place a grid of dots and connect them with straight or geometric lines to form stars, squares, or flowers.
Where it originated: Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh (Central India).

The Origin Story: This practice began among the pastoral and royal communities of Central India. Rather than drawing lines to trap spirits, it developed as floor painting (dhuli citra) to decorate courtyards for festivals and royal celebrations. Without a strict dot grid, people used their fingers to draw freehand animals, flowers, and symbols, filling them with vivid colored powder to resemble royal carpets.
Early Tamil Sangam literature refers to decorated entrances and courtyards, showing that floor decoration was practiced during that period.
During festivals and special occasions, Kolams are made larger and more elaborate to mark celebrations and welcome visitors.
A Playground for Modern Computer Science
In the 1970s and 1980s, computer scientists at Madras Christian College, led by Dr. Gift Siromoney, made a breakthrough: they recognized that Sikku Kolams are advanced visual algorithms.
They discovered that the rules used to loop lines around dots closely match formal picture languages and array grammars used in computer programming.
Today, researchers worldwide use Kolam structures to study knot theory, picture logic, DNA splicing models, and advanced robotics trajectory planning.
Kolam is traditionally associated with a time called Brahma Muhurtam, an auspicious period beginning about 1.5 hours before sunrise.
Culturally, people believed deities passed over the earth at this time and would bypass a home with an empty threshold.
Anthropologically, it served as a social signal: a freshly drawn Kolam told the village that the women of the household were awake and safe, and that the home was ready to welcome the community.
Explore glimpses of traditional Tamil village life in our collection of historical photographs.
